title: Resisting change
log: 2026-11-01T08:04:35Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: Neither bank point covers the new point's specific idea that governments and powerful groups use laws, police, propaganda and violence to resist movements for change; they describe resistance by businesses or by groups in general, and the social card's broader focus is a different idea at a different depth.

draft.title: Resisting change
card: Movements for change often threaten people who hold power. Governments and other powerful groups may act to protect their position and the existing order.
rules that ban or limit a movement, or keep a group out of power. South Africa's apartheid government banned the African National Congress in 1960.
arrests, bans on meetings and violence used to break up protests. At Sharpeville in 1960, South African police shot into a crowd of protesters.
messages that shape opinion, such as claiming a movement is dangerous or foreign. Resistance often used several of these tools together.
draft.remember: Those with power can resist change through laws, force and propaganda, and often use more than one.

a.q: A government bans a protest group, then runs newspaper stories calling its members dangerous. What does this show?
opts: Resistance to change using law and propaganda
A movement using media to win public support
A government agreeing to a movement's demands
A movement using legal action to gain rights
a.why: The ban is a law used against the group, and the stories are propaganda meant to turn opinion against it. Media use by a movement is different, because here the government is the one acting to block change.
a.clue: Ask who is using the tools, and what they want.

b.q: In 1960, police in Sharpeville, South Africa, fired on a crowd protesting against the pass laws. The government then banned the ANC. Which best describes these actions?
opts: Force and law used together to resist change
Propaganda used to win over the protesters
Non-violent protest used by the government
Legal action brought by the movement
b.why: Shooting at the crowd was force, and banning the ANC was a law used to limit the movement. The two worked together. Propaganda is about shaping opinion, and neither action does that.
b.clue: Look for what the police did and what the government passed.

a.best: Resistance to change using law and propaganda

b.best: Force and law used together to resist change

problems.detail: The right option is the only one that mentions resisting change, echoing the card's title, and it is slightly the longest. The distractors are weak: 'Non-violent protest used by the government' makes no sense, and 'Legal action brought by the movement' plainly does not fit a government action. A student could pick the answer without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The facts check out: Sharpeville and the banning of the ANC both happened in 1960. Question b's distractors are implausible, and its right option is the only one that echoes the title, so it is easy to guess.

b.q: In 1963, officials in Birmingham, Alabama, got a court order banning civil rights marches. When marchers went ahead, police turned fire hoses and dogs on them. Which tools were used?
opts: A legal ban, then police force
b.why: The court order was a legal rule that banned the marches, and the hoses and dogs were force used to break them up. Propaganda is tempting because officials wanted to stop the movement, but neither action was a message meant to shape opinion.
b.clue: Which action was a rule, and which was physical?
